did_you_know.text: Job asks his friends to listen to him all the way through, viewing the act of listening itself as a consolation: “Listen carefully to my words.”
Job asks his friends to look at him in astonishment and put their hands over their mouths—an expression of silence and shock at the harshness of his words.
The central question Job raises in this chapter is why the wicked continue to live, grow old, and become strong, even though they seemingly deserve punishment.
Job describes the lives of the wicked as lives of prosperity and abundance, but emphasizes that the transition from life to the grave may happen “in a moment.”
According to Job’s description, the wicked do not merely distance themselves from God; they even say to him openly, “Leave us alone,” and have no desire to know his ways.
Job asks rhetorically how often the lamp of the wicked is truly extinguished and disaster comes upon them. In this way, he challenges the idea that divine punishment is always visible and immediate.
Job emphasizes the gap between human knowledge and God’s knowledge: people cannot teach God anything, since God is the judge even of the exalted and lofty.

Job contrasts two people: one dies peacefully, satisfied and healthy, while the other dies bitter in spirit without enjoying any prosperity. The contrast shows that there is no simple pattern of reward and punishment in this world.

Job points his friends to the testimony of travelers, who know that even the wicked may be spared on the day of disaster and preserved for the day of wrath. Therefore, one should not always infer a person’s righteousness or wickedness from their circumstances.

Even after his death, the wicked person is described as being carried to the grave and receiving an honored resting place on a burial mound. In this way, Job rejects the claim that every wicked person is immediately exposed in disgrace.
